content: Vaginal Discharge and Associated Conditions 1. Trichomoniasis (T. vaginalis) Trichomonas vaginalis is a sexually transmitted protozoan that infects the vagina, urethra, and paraurethral glands in women. While many women remain asymptomatic, over 50% of those infected experience vaginal discharge. Symptomatic women often report abnormal vaginal discharge, which may be yellow and purulent, and about half experience vulvar itching. On examination, vulvar erythema and edema may be observed. Speculum examination may reveal a frothy, yellow or greenish discharge, and the vaginal walls may appear erythematous. A strawberry cervix, characterized by punctate hemorrhages on the cervix, is a rare but highly indicative finding of trichomoniasis. Diagnostic methods include: Molecular Testing (NAAT): This is the most sensitive diagnostic method. Vaginal swabs are preferred, but endocervical samples and urine can also be used. NAAT is not widely available as a rapid point-of-care test but can be strategically implemented where resources allow. Microscopy (Wet Mount): This method is quick and inexpensive but requires immediate examination (within 10 minutes) to detect motile trichomonads. Non-motile cells cannot confirm the diagnosis. Culture Methods: Previously the gold standard, culture methods are more sensitive than wet mount microscopy but are less commonly used today due to the availability of advanced diagnostic techniques. 2. Candidiasis Vulvovaginal candidiasis is caused by Candida albicans in approximately 90% of cases, with non-albicans species such as Candida glabrata, Candida tropicalis, and others accounting for the remainder. While men can be transiently colonized with Candida, conditions like Candida balanitis are not considered sexually transmitted infections. Candida species are detected in 20–30% of asymptomatic women of childbearing age, and treatment is not always necessary in these cases. Symptoms include vulvar itching, burning, soreness, and irritation. Pain during intercourse (dyspareunia) and urination (dysuria) may also occur. The discharge is typically thick, white, and curd-like but can vary in consistency. Examination findings may include erythema, swelling, and excoriation of the vulva, with curd-like or homogeneous white discharge adherent to the vaginal walls. The cervix usually appears normal. Diagnostic methods include: Microscopy: A Gram stain of vaginal secretions can demonstrate gram-positive Candida species. A potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation is also useful for identifying yeast cells. Culture Methods: Candida culture is the most sensitive diagnostic test but requires up to three days for results, delaying treatment. 3. Bacterial Vaginosis (BV) Bacterial vaginosis is the most common cause of vaginal discharge in women of childbearing age. It is a polymicrobial condition characterized by a reduction or absence of lactobacilli and an overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria. Approximately 90% of symptomatic women report a thin, white vaginal discharge and an abnormal odor. Examination findings include a thin, homogeneous discharge that may adhere to the vaginal walls. The cervix typically appears normal. A whiff test using potassium hydroxide (KOH) may reveal a fishy odor, which is subjective and not always discernible. Diagnostic methods include: Microscopy: Wet mount microscopy can identify clue cells, which are vaginal epithelial cells coated with bacteria. Gram-stained vaginal smears can also reveal a reduction in lactobacilli and the presence of gram-positive and gram-negative cocci. pH Testing: Elevated vaginal pH can support the diagnosis but may be affected by external factors such as recent douching or menstruation. 4. Cervical Infections (Gonococcal and/or Chlamydial Cervicitis) Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis primarily infect the endocervix and may cause cervical discharge that manifests as vaginal discharge. These pathogens are less commonly associated with vaginal discharge but are significant causes of sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Risk factors for cervical infections include being under 21 years of age, having multiple or new sexual partners, and having a partner with an STI. At least 50% of women with gonococcal or chlamydial infections are asymptomatic. Symptomatic women may experience vaginal discharge, abnormal bleeding, dysuria, or lower abdominal pain due to ascending infection (pelvic inflammatory disease). Examination findings may include a normal cervix or one that is erythematous, eroded, and associated with mucopurulent discharge. The cervix may bleed easily upon contact. Diagnostic methods include: Molecular Testing: NAAT is the gold standard for detecting N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. Self-collected vaginal swabs or clinician-collected endocervical swabs are preferred. First-catch urine is an alternative but less sensitive in women. Microscopy: Gram-stained cervical smears can identify intracellular gram-negative diplococci, indicative of gonorrhea, but this method has low sensitivity in women. 5. In settings without access to molecular testing, treatment may be guided by clinical findings, risk factors, and rapid point-of-care tests. Treatment recommendations include: Trichomoniasis and Bacterial Vaginosis: Metronidazole is effective for both conditions. Candidiasis: Options include topical antifungals (e.g., miconazole, clotrimazole) or oral fluconazole. Cervical Infections: Dual therapy with ceftriaxone and azithromycin is recommended for gonorrhea and chlamydia. Doxycycline is an alternative for chlamydia. In resource-limited settings, syndromic management may be employed, treating for multiple potential infections simultaneously. However, this approach may lead to overtreatment or missed cases. 6. Good Practices For recurrent or persistent vaginal discharge, referral to a center with laboratory capacity for advanced diagnostics is recommended. This includes testing for antimicrobial-resistant N. gonorrhoeae and M. genitalium. Offering HIV and syphilis testing and other preventive services is also encouraged. In summary, the management of vaginal discharge requires a combination of clinical assessment, diagnostic testing, and appropriate treatment tailored to the resources available. Molecular testing offers the highest accuracy but may not be feasible in all settings. Syndromic management remains a practical alternative in resource-limited environments.
